blocks.x: Driving to the Amalfi Coast from Naples along a series of hairpin cliffside turns worthy of the finest of Formula 1 drivers, I found myself mimicking a child on a road trip, asking the same question on repeat: “Are we there yet?” It didn’t take long before I was distracted by the lush Lattari Mountains, whose staggering peaks are blanketed in forests as verdant as what you’d expect on a tropical island like Tahiti. Thick chestnut trees slowly morphed into neatly manicured terraces of olive trees, vineyards, and lemon groves as I ventured closer to the coast. “The most important monument here is the landscape,” the driver said as we squeezed along a narrow bend beside a bus. He also assured me that Ravello—considered the “jewel in the crown” of the Amalfi Coast, where merchant aristocrats constructed cliffside palazzi and composers like Richard Wagner found inspiration—was only five minutes away.

The Amalfi Coast may be located near renowned ruins like Pompeii—and sits catty-corner from the the glitzy island of Capri and its famous Blue Grotto—but the 30-mile stretch of coastline in Campania earned its own UNESCO status thanks to a blend of Tetris-like cliffside towns, Arab and Byzantine architecture, and signature stone terraces producing the region’s prized “yellow gold,” or lemons. “I think one of the reasons Amalfi continues to be such a perennial destination is that it has never been only about the view— the landscape is extraordinary, but Amalfi has a depth of history and culture that you can still feel when you walk through the town,” says Alessandro Mansi, owner of Amalfi’s cliffside Hotel Miramalfi. “I think this balance between heritage and evolution is what makes the Amalfi Coast particularly interesting right now—it is no longer simply a place to come for the views and spend a few days by the sea; there is an increasing appetite among travelers to discover the history, food, craftsmanship, people, and traditions behind the destination.”

Running along the tip of the Sorrentine Peninsula, from Vietri sul Mare in the east to Positano, the Amalfi Drive strings together a majority of the coastline’s 13 towns. While the drive is dubbed one of the world’s most scenic, if you’re not familiar with Italy’s narrow mountain roads (or drivers, for that matter), skip renting a car and explore the region by ferry, taxi, or the main bus line, SITA SUD, instead. Another option? The Path of the Gods hike, a 4.3-mile former shepherd’s trail that ends just above Positano—and you can descend down 1,700 timeworn stone steps to the seaside town below.

Amalfi was one of Italy's four historic Maritime Republics, together with Venice, Genoa, and Pisa, and that heritage is still celebrated today with the annual May Regatta of the Ancient Maritime Republics, when traditional galleons representing the four cities compete. “The spirit of the small Italian villages of the south stay true to themselves and remain authentic in their atmosphere,” says Mariella Avino, co-owner and managing director of Ravello’s Palazzo Avino. “This is thanks to the strong spirit of the people who live along the coast full time, who are very conscious to keep the heart of the places alive and unchanged.”

Whether you’re visiting in the midst of summer or savoring the seaside in spring or early fall during festival season, here’s how to plan a trip to the Amalfi Coast—and where to go when you want to see a more local side.
